contracts.text: For wave 1, simulation/run.py exposes run(settings), returning a dict with processed_samples, limited, bands, desired, residual and output. It accepts JSON-compatible settings for a single tone and fixed filter; the settings example and exact supported fixed-filter fields must be documented in the module before implementation consumers are wired. Arrays contain one numeric sample per processed sample; desired is the signal before cancellation, output is simulated anti-noise, and residual is the remaining error. The function does not persist or assign an ID. Invalid settings raise ValueError with a useful message. Wave 2 extends this same interface for the supplied LMS example and other valid tones and band-noise settings.

A saved and exposed session is JSON with id, settings, status (running, completed or stopped), limited (boolean), processed_samples, bands [{low, high, attenuation_db}], and desired, residual and output sample arrays. Wave 1 saves the original settings and completed fixed-filter result under a stable ID; list and show return that same session representation. Preserve wave-1 JSON as legacy input in later waves. An unavailable attenuation is JSON null, not a fabricated number.

Run locally as python server.py --port PORT --data DIR; serve the page and assets from the same local origin without external services. POST /api/runs accepts a JSON settings object and, for wave 1, returns the completed session JSON; GET /api/sessions returns a JSON array of sessions; GET /api/sessions/ID returns that session. Invalid requests return a non-success status and a readable JSON error. Later waves may return a running session asynchronously.

python bench.py run --data DIR --settings JSON and python bench.py show ID --data DIR emit session JSON; python bench.py list --data DIR emits a JSON array; python bench.py export ID --data DIR emits CSV. JSON is the settings argument, not an assumed filename. Successful machine-readable output goes to stdout and errors go to stderr with a nonzero exit. CLI and server use the same data directory and session representation.

The backend serves page/index.html at / and the files under page/ at corresponding same-origin paths. The page uses relative API and asset URLs; no network-hosted assets or runtime packages are required. Wave 1 provides a labelled textarea[name=settings], a Start run button, and saved-session buttons with data-session-id set to the session ID; selecting one displays its ID, settings and result.
Wave 2 agreement: define reproducible band energy, boundary and unavailable-value semantics shared by saved results, explanations and comparison.
Wave 3 agreement: compare saved bands with delta_db equal to B minus A and expose enough run context to judge comparability.
Wave 3 agreement: cooperative stop, partial results and limiter reporting must preserve actual processed samples and bounded stored output.

dream:
Build Quiet Bench, a noise-cancelling test bench that runs on this PC with no audio hardware. Python 3.12 standard library plus Node 20
for the page checks; no third-party runtime packages, no network. I can generate a noise signal (tones, band noise) or import a WAV
file; the bench simulates the acoustic path from the noise source to the ear, runs an adaptive canceller (LMS family) against it and
tells me how much was cancelled in each frequency band. Every session is saved on a small local storage server
(`python server.py --port PORT --data DIR`) with its settings and results, and a web page on that server lets me start a run, browse
saved sessions, reload one and compare two. A command line (`python bench.py run|list|show|export`) does the same without the page.
A limiter must hold the output inside a safe level when the filter diverges, and a stop switch ends a run at once.
Build it in three waves and show me each one. Wave 1: the thinnest thing that runs end to end, one tone through a fixed filter,
saved and shown. Wave 2: the adaptive filter, attenuation per band, browse and reload. Wave 3: compare runs, limiter and stop
switch, WAV import.
